headline: Cannabis research: CBD autism trial finds limited gains in boys
dek: A UC San Diego trial found CBD beat placebo only on motor skills in 30 boys with profound autism; a Canadian study compared private and state shops.
key_points: A secondary analysis of a randomised, double-blind trial at UC San Diego found no significant difference between CBD and placebo on most measures of adaptive functioning.
CBD was better than placebo on motor skills, a gap driven largely by motor scores worsening during the placebo period.
Communication scores improved from baseline on CBD but not on placebo; the authors call for larger trials that account for placebo effects.
University of Regina economists found private cannabis retail in Canada offers more variety and stores than government retail, at nearly the same price.
body: Two peer-reviewed papers this week test claims that are often made with more confidence than the evidence supports: that cannabidiol (CBD) helps children with autism, and that government-run cannabis shops serve consumers as well as private ones. The first finds a small, specific benefit inside a mostly negative result. The second finds that price is the one thing the two retail models have in common.
Neither paper is the last word. The autism study is small and reports secondary outcomes. The retail study is a two-day snapshot. Both are useful mainly for what they rule out.
## CBD in boys with profound autism

The autism paper was published online on 18 November in the Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders by a team at the University of California San Diego. Its title states the finding plainly: limited efficacy of cannabidiol on adaptive functioning in boys with profound autism.

The study reports a secondary outcome from a randomised, double-blind trial of purified CBD against placebo, whose primary results were published in 2025. Adaptive functioning, meaning everyday skills such as communication, daily living, socialising and movement, was measured with the Vineland Adaptive Behavior Scales, Third Edition. Because many participants scored at the bottom of the standard scale, a floor effect, the researchers also analysed raw scores.

The Marijuana Herald, which reported on the paper, said the analysis covered 30 boys aged 7 to 14, about 73% of them non-verbal. They received pharmaceutical-grade CBD (Epidiolex) at up to 20 milligrams per kilogram of body weight a day and placebo in separate eight-week periods, with a four-week washout between them.
## What the trial found

According to the abstract, there were no significant differences between CBD and placebo on adaptive functioning after eight weeks, with one exception: motor skills, where CBD was superior on both standard and raw scores. The abstract also shows where that gap came from. Compared with its own starting point, placebo was associated with worsening motor scores. The Herald's report adds that CBD did not produce a statistically significant motor improvement from baseline, so the difference reflects decline on placebo more than gain on CBD.

Within the CBD period, raw scores for receptive communication (understanding speech) and written communication improved from baseline, and expressive communication and personal skills came close to significance. Placebo showed no such communication gains, though it was associated with an improvement in a community-skills measure. These are within-group changes. They are not the same as showing CBD beat placebo on communication, and the trial did not show that.
> In this trial CBD beat placebo on one measure out of many, and the authors put the word limited in their own title.

The authors conclude that future studies should account for placebo effects and symptom severity, enrol more participants and include people across a range of severity. The Herald notes that the original 2025 report found a substantial placebo effect and no significant difference between treatments on the primary behavioural measures. The paper's conflict-of-interest statement says the corresponding author, D. Trauner, was a site investigator for a separate, industry-sponsored multicentre CBD trial in 2023, after this work was completed.
## What it means for the CBD market

For companies selling CBD, the study supports a narrow statement at most: in one small trial of a prescription-grade product at high doses, there were signals in communication worth testing further. It does not support claims that CBD treats autism, and it says nothing about over-the-counter hemp CBD products, which differ in dose and purity. This is a summary of research, not medical advice; treatment decisions belong with a child's clinicians.
## Private shops versus government shops in Canada

The second paper, in the Journal of Cannabis Research, comes from two economists at the University of Regina, Jason Childs and K. Christ, and compares retail systems across Canadian provinces. Canada legalised adult-use cannabis in 2018 and let each province choose its retail model. Some chose competing private shops, some a government monopoly or government-dominated system, some a hybrid.

The authors collected prices and product listings from public retail websites over two consecutive days in June 2024: the single website of each government retailer, and each location of 11 major private chains in provinces with fully private retail. Store counts came from provincial regulators. The Herald reports that the private group was Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba and Ontario, and the government group Quebec, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island.

The result: no significant difference in price between the two systems. The Herald gives the averages as C$6.46 a gram in private markets and C$6.50 in government ones. Variety and convenience were significantly higher under private retail, and private-retail provinces had at least nearly three times as many stores per 10,000 residents, according to the Herald. The abstract notes that provinces that began with private retail have done better at displacing the illegal market, and suggests variety and access, not price, may explain why.
## What it means for US states

The finding lines up with the Yale analysis of Washington state we covered on 19 November, which estimated that more retail licences would lower prices and benefit buyers. Together the two papers point the same way: the number and range of legal shops matters to whether consumers use them. The Canadian study has clear limits. It is a snapshot, not a record of what people bought, and it compares listed prices, not purchases. It also cannot separate retail model from other provincial differences such as wholesale rules.

The question is live in the United States. State-run stores have featured in some US legalisation debates. This paper suggests a state-store model would not necessarily raise prices, but would likely offer fewer products and fewer outlets, which may leave more room for unlicensed sellers. That inference is ours.
## What to watch

Watch for larger, multi-site CBD trials in autism that use placebo-controlled designs across severity levels, as the UC San Diego authors recommend. In retail policy, watch the 2027 legislative sessions in states weighing legalisation models, and any follow-up Canadian work that links store density and variety to measured declines in illicit sales.
